slides.title: Newborn seahorses already capture live prey
body: Newborn lined seahorses, _Hippocampus erectus_, capture live **Artemia**, small crustaceans used as food, immediately after leaving the male. Their feeding behavior already combines visual search, target tracking, rapid head rotation, and ingestion. Feeding competence therefore begins before the feeding skeleton reaches its later degree of ossification.

Sun and colleagues recorded animals from 1 to 30 days after parturition, meaning birth. Newborns were about 9.2 mm tall and successfully captured prey in about 77% of feeding attempts under the study conditions.

Across development, body growth increased capture reach and food intake. Early independence depends on functional sensory and motor coordination together with continued maturation of the snout and digestive tract.

slides.title: Prey capture combines four coordinated actions
body: **Pivot feeding** brings the mouth toward prey by rotating the head upward, followed by suction into the tubular snout. In newborn lined seahorses, this behavior formed a sequence of searching, locking, capturing, and swallowing. Each action changes the relationship between the animal and its target.

During searching, the eyes moved independently. During locking, the seahorse swam and turned to keep the prey ahead of its head. Capture began when the target entered the available capture distance, with head rotation and mouth opening taking less than 4 ms.

Swallowing restored the cranial and hyoid apparatus toward rest while ingested water and fragments exited through the gill opening. Fast acquisition and slower recovery are distinct components of the same feeding sequence.

slides.title: Independent eye movements precede target tracking
body: The two eyes of juvenile lined seahorses moved independently during prey search. After prey entered the visual field, the animal changed its swimming and turning so that the target remained in front of the head. These observations separate broad searching movements from target-directed tracking.

The newborn eye already contained an organized retina, the neural tissue that receives light. Rod and cone photoreceptors were present, together with a pigmented outer region and recognizable internal layers. The sensory tissue was therefore developed when independent feeding began.

Target tracking and the final strike operated on different time scales. Swimming maintained alignment before the brief capture movement, which could then bring the small terminal mouth to a nearby crustacean.

slides.title: Photoreceptors are present at birth
body: **Photoreceptors** are retinal cells specialized to receive light. Histological sections of newborn lined seahorses contained both rods and cones between the pigment layer and the outer nuclear layer. The pigment layer and organized retinal tissue were already recognizable on the first day after birth.

Sun and colleagues used 4 µm tissue sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Their labeled sections distinguish photoreceptor tissue, nuclear layers, the ganglion-cell region, lens, and other ocular structures. This preparation describes tissue organization rather than directly measuring visual resolution.
The same newborn animals performed successful visual prey capture. Retinal differentiation and feeding competence therefore coexist at release, while later growth enlarges an already organized eye.

slides.title: Eye growth preserves the early retinal organization
body: From 3 to 30 days after birth, juvenile lined seahorse eyes increased in diameter as the animals grew. Sun and colleagues reported no major rearrangement of the retinal histology during this period. Growth enlarged the organ while preserving its recognizable internal organization.

The retina was therefore unlike a sensory system that acquires its basic tissue layers only after feeding begins. At birth, the animal already combined an organized eye with successful capture; later increases in capture performance occurred while the existing retinal architecture remained recognizable.

Feeding development involved several tissues at once. Eye enlargement accompanied snout growth, increasing attack distance, and maturation of the digestive tract, so behavioral improvement belonged to the developing animal as a whole.

slides.title: The seahorse brain retains five major divisions
body: The brain of _Hippocampus barbouri_ contains the **telencephalon**, forebrain tissue including the cerebral hemispheres; the diencephalon; the mesencephalon or midbrain; the metencephalon; and the myelencephalon. Senarat and colleagues identified these divisions in sagittal histological sections, which cut along the head-to-tail axis.

The diencephalon contains the hypothalamus, while the midbrain contains the optic tectum. The metencephalon includes the cerebellum, and the myelencephalon includes the medulla, which continues toward the spinal cord. The unusual external body shape therefore accompanies a recognizable teleost brain arrangement.
The study compared tissue organization from 1 to 35 days after birth. Early sections were compact, whereas later sections distinguished the regional and cellular features of these divisions.

slides.title: The optic tectum is a prominent brain region
body: The **optic tectum**, a midbrain region associated with visual orientation and multisensory processing in fishes, was the most prominent gross brain region in the examined _Hippocampus barbouri_. It lay between the anterior cerebral hemispheres and the posterior cerebellum.

Senarat and colleagues combined dissections, photographs, measurements, and stained tissue sections. In their 35-day animals, the tectum measured about 1,220 µm in length, compared with a cerebellar length of about 714 µm. These measurements describe regional anatomy in that developmental sample.

The authors proposed that the prominent tectum relates to visually guided feeding on mobile prey. This is an anatomical hypothesis connecting brain organization to behavior, rather than a recorded seahorse visual-neuron response.

slides.title: The tectum contains five histological layers
body: **Laminar organization** means that neural tissue is arranged in layers with different cellular and fiber composition. Senarat and colleagues recognized five layers in the seahorse optic tectum: stratum marginale, stratum opticum, stratum album centrale, stratum griseum centrale, and stratum periventriculare.

These layers extend from the outer tectal surface toward the ventricular region. Their differences in neuronal density and fiber organization divide the tissue into distinct anatomical compartments. The published micrographs preserve this organization at a scale of tens of micrometers.
The five-layer pattern was clear by 35 days after birth. Earlier tissue was less differentiated, so the layered tectum emerged during postnatal brain development while the animal continued growing.

slides.title: Tectal vascularization increases during development
body: **Capillaries** are small blood vessels supplying tissues. In _Hippocampus barbouri_, tectal capillaries became more apparent at 6 days after birth, and small vessels were conspicuous by 14 days. At 35 days, the tectum was highly vascularized and its five layers were distinguishable.

Senarat and colleagues followed these changes in stained sections. Vascular development occurred together with regional differentiation, linking the growth of neural tissue to the organization of its blood supply. The two features progressed within the same developmental sequence.

The authors hypothesized that increasing brain differentiation supports developing predatory ability. The age-dependent vascular and tissue changes provide an anatomical description of maturation, while prey-capture timing requires the separate behavioral evidence.

slides.title: The cerebellum has three distinct cellular layers
body: The **cerebellum** lies behind the optic tectum in the seahorse brain. In 35-day _Hippocampus barbouri_, it contained an outer molecular layer, a Purkinje-cell layer, and an inner granular layer. This organization separates dendritic tissue from identifiable neuronal populations.

The molecular layer contained many dendritic fibers. **Dendrites** are neuronal processes that receive synaptic input. Synapses are junctions through which neurons communicate. The middle layer contained conspicuous Purkinje cells, while the granular layer contained densely arranged smaller principal neurons. Senarat and colleagues identified these regions using light microscopy.

Cerebellar differentiation continued after birth rather than appearing fully mature in the youngest animals. Increasing prominence of Purkinje cells and their dendrites accompanied the emergence of the layered tissue organization.

slides.title: Purkinje cells become conspicuous after birth
body: **Purkinje cells** are the large neurons occupying the middle layer of the cerebellar cortex. They were difficult to identify in the earliest _Hippocampus barbouri_ sections, became apparent by 14 days after birth, and were prominent by 35 days.

The later cells possessed dendrites extending into the molecular layer, where the study described abundant dendritic fibers. Development therefore involved the emergence of recognizable neuronal shape as well as separation of the three cerebellar layers.

This cellular sequence occurred while tectal layers and blood vessels also became more distinct. Different neural regions matured over overlapping postnatal intervals, producing a more differentiated brain rather than a single abrupt anatomical transition.

slides.title: Olfactory tissue occupies the anterior snout
body: **Olfactory epithelium** is sensory tissue associated with chemical detection. In _Hippocampus barbouri_, Senarat and colleagues identified olfactory tissue in the anterior snout, surrounding a cavity and containing ciliated sensory cells. The cilia were conspicuous in the higher-magnification sections.

The olfactory tract connected the anterior olfactory region with the forebrain. A **tract** is a bundle of nerve fibers linking regions. Gross and histological preparations therefore located both the peripheral sensory tissue and its connection toward the cerebral hemispheres.

Vision dominates the published prey-tracking observations, but the seahorse head also contains a distinct chemical-sensory apparatus. These sensory structures occupy different anatomical locations and can contribute different kinds of information during interactions with the environment.

slides.title: The diencephalon includes endocrine-associated tissue
body: The **diencephalon** lies beneath the midbrain and contains the epithalamus, thalamus, and hypothalamus. Senarat and colleagues distinguished these regions in stained _Hippocampus barbouri_ sections. The hypothalamus was the dominant portion of this division in their anatomical description.

The three diencephalic regions occupied distinct positions beneath the midbrain. The thalamus lay between the epithalamus and hypothalamus and contained neuronal cell bodies, supporting glial cells, and nerve fibers. **Glial cells** are non-neuronal cells that support neural tissue; they were recognizable alongside neurons in several brain regions.

The hypothalamus contained neurosecretory cell populations and was anatomically associated with the pituitary. This regional arrangement places hormone-related tissue within the same brain that contains the visual and motor-associated structures.

slides.title: Hypothalamic and pituitary tissues are differentiated
body: **Neurosecretory cells** are neural cells specialized to produce secreted signaling molecules. Senarat and colleagues described such cell populations in the seahorse hypothalamus, including periventricular and lateral tuberal regions. These locations differed from the layered optic tectum and cerebellum.

The pituitary contained a neural region, the **neurohypophysis**, and a glandular region, the adenohypophysis. Histological sections distinguished their tissue organization, providing an anatomical basis for separating neural hormone-associated tissue from glandular endocrine tissue.

During development, pituitary glandular tissue became conspicuous by 14 days after birth. Neural, vascular, and endocrine-associated structures therefore differentiated over overlapping intervals, while later reproductive experiments examined how peptide signals altered pituitary gene expression.

slides.title: The hindbrain continues into the spinal cord
body: The **medulla oblongata** is the posterior brain region that continues toward the spinal cord. In _Hippocampus barbouri_, the medulla contained neurons and glial cells, with the fourth ventricle bordering part of the tissue. Senarat and colleagues followed this continuity in sagittal sections.

The spinal cord extended through the vertebral column. Cross-sections contained central neural tissue and a central canal, the fluid-containing channel continuous with the brain ventricles. The canal boundary included ependymal cells, which line these internal fluid spaces.

The brain and spinal cord form a continuous central nervous system. Within spinal tissue, neurons and glial cells occupied the region surrounding the central canal, extending cellular organization along the brain-to-body axis.

slides.title: Neural maturation and feeding competence differ
body: Newborn _Hippocampus barbouri_ brains appeared compact, with relatively indistinct substructures, in Senarat and colleagues’ sections. By contrast, Sun and colleagues observed organized retinas and successful prey capture on the first day after birth in lined seahorses, _Hippocampus erectus_.

These findings concern different species and different measurements. **Behavioral competence** means successful performance of an action, whereas histological differentiation describes the visibility and organization of tissue features. A functional behavior can occur while anatomical maturation continues.

The brain study’s proposed onset of predatory development at 6–14 days is therefore a species-specific anatomical hypothesis. Direct newborn feeding observations establish early competence in the lined seahorse and identify continued development as improvement of an existing behavior.

slides.title: The newborn feeding skeleton is largely cartilaginous
body: **Cartilage** forms much of the early feeding skeleton in juvenile lined seahorses. body: **Feeding caliber** is the maximum snout width reached during suction feeding. Sun and colleagues compared this width with the resting snout width to describe expansion. Newborn lined seahorses expanded to about 216% of their resting width, whereas the value was about 106% by day 14.

body: Newborn lined seahorses had a short, relatively straight intestine with a thin mucosal layer. **Mucosa** is the inner tissue lining the digestive lumen. During the first postnatal days, folds and loops developed, increasing the complexity of the organ that receives captured food.

slides.title: A slow predator can approach evasive copepods
body: Dwarf seahorses, _Hippocampus zosterae_, capture **copepods**, small swimming crustaceans that detect disturbances in the surrounding water. Gemmell and colleagues studied approaches to _Acartia tonsa_ using high-speed holography, a method that reconstructs positions and particle movement within a three-dimensional sample volume.

About 84% of approaches brought the copepod within roughly 1 mm without triggering escape. Once prey entered capture range, capture succeeded about 94% of the time. Successful feeding therefore combined an undetected approach with an exceptionally rapid final strike.
The approach and strike solve different problems. Slow positioning limits the warning available to the prey, while head rotation rapidly closes the remaining short distance.

slides.title: Successful approaches were slower than failed ones
body: Approach speed differed between successful and failed dwarf-seahorse feeding attempts. Gemmell and colleagues measured successful approaches at about 8.4 mm/s and unsuccessful approaches at about 14.1 mm/s. These values describe the movement before the final pivot-feeding strike.

A moving head deforms the surrounding water. **Hydrodynamic disturbance** is the resulting change in water motion that a mechanosensitive prey animal can detect. Faster approaches increased the disturbance near the region where the copepod would eventually be captured.

The seahorse’s short-range strike therefore depended on careful preceding positioning. Rapid final acquisition was compatible with a slower approach, because minimizing the prey’s warning and minimizing the final capture time require different movement patterns.

slides.title: The final strike outruns a copepod response
body: High-speed recordings at 2,000 frames/s resolved the final dwarf-seahorse strike. The mouth covered the remaining distance to the copepod in less than 1 ms. The source contrasts this interval with copepod escape-response latencies of approximately 2–4 ms reported in earlier work.

**Response latency** is the time between detection of a stimulus and the beginning of a response. A strike completed before that interval expires can acquire the prey before an effective escape movement develops. The advantage depends on beginning within the very short capture range.

slides.title: A quiet water region lies above the snout
body: **Particle tracking** follows small suspended tracers to estimate local water movement. Gemmell and colleagues used live diatoms as tracers during dwarf-seahorse approaches and reconstructed their positions holographically. Water motion above the snout was lower than in adjacent regions.

Within the measured capture region, water velocities did not exceed about 0.8 mm/s, whereas neighboring regions reached about 4.1 mm/s. The prey could occupy a comparatively quiet zone even though the moving predator disturbed water elsewhere around its head.

This spatial pattern connects head form with prey detection. The mouth rotates toward the zone during capture, so the location with reduced warning also lies within the range reached by pivot feeding.

body: Gemmell and colleagues placed preserved dwarf-seahorse heads in a flow chamber and measured water movement with **particle image velocimetry**, which estimates velocity from displacement of illuminated particles. Imposed flow represented the relative movement occurring during an approach.

body: **Posture** determines which surfaces of the seahorse head meet the incoming water. Different feeding anatomies therefore create different sensory conditions for prey. The seahorse places its capture region within a low-disturbance zone, whereas the stickleback’s frontal region remains comparatively exposed to deformation.

slides.title: Pairing changes the context of visual interaction
body: Mederos and colleagues paired male and female lined seahorses for 5 days, then tested interactions with the familiar partner and an opposite-sex stranger. The animals occupied separate sections of a test tank, allowing their brightness changes to be analyzed during proximity to either individual.

**Luminance** describes brightness in a visual channel rather than hue, the kind of color perceived. The researchers calibrated video images and evaluated changes in abdominal luminance using a seahorse visual model. Partner interactions produced larger and more correlated changes than stranger interactions.

The measured social response was context-dependent brightening. Familiarity with a specific individual altered visual interaction even when both available animals were potential opposite-sex social partners.

body: After behavioral testing, Mederos and colleagues extracted **RNA**, the molecules carrying gene transcripts, from individual whole brains. body: **Orthologous genes** are corresponding genes inherited from a shared ancestor. slides.title: Kisspeptin signaling is concentrated in the brain
body: **Kisspeptin** is a peptide signal associated with reproductive regulation. Zhang and colleagues identified a kiss2 gene and its receptor gene, GPR54-2, in lined seahorses. Their tissue measurements found kiss2 transcripts in several locations, including brain and gonadal tissue.

GPR54-2 transcripts were concentrated in the brain and close to the detection limit in peripheral tissues. Within the brain, both ligand and receptor transcripts were especially abundant in the hypothalamic region. The complementary distribution places a peptide-producing system and a potential responding system in reproductive neural tissue.

Female brains contained higher transcript levels than male brains in the reported comparison. Sex and reproductive state therefore influence the molecular organization of the same named kisspeptin signaling system.

slides.title: Brain Kiss2 rises near the onset of puberty
body: **Puberty** is the developmental transition toward reproductive competence. Zhang and colleagues followed male lined seahorses from immature animals at 3 months through early puberty at 4 months, advanced puberty at 5 months, and maturity at 6 months. Testis histology distinguished these developmental stages.

Brain kiss2 transcript abundance was highest around early puberty, while testis kiss2 showed no comparable developmental change. The difference places the stage-associated molecular signal primarily in the brain within the tissues examined.

The gonads continued maturing as the animals aged. Brain transcript change and testicular differentiation therefore describe complementary parts of reproductive development, with the kisspeptin system positioned as a candidate regulator of the transition rather than merely a marker of adult body size.

slides.title: Pregnancy reduces Kiss2-associated transcripts
body: Zhang and colleagues compared male lined seahorses before pregnancy, during pregnancy, and after birth. **Pregnancy** in seahorses is the period of paternal incubation following egg transfer and fertilization. Brain and testis kiss2 transcripts decreased during that stage and returned toward preceding levels after birth.

Brain GPR54-2 transcripts also decreased during pregnancy. Ligand and receptor expression therefore changed together across the reproductive cycle in the sampled tissues. The same peptide system associated with puberty was reorganized during an adult reproductive state.

The authors hypothesized that reduced reproductive signaling during pregnancy relates to the temporary reproductive cycle. The observed return after birth identifies molecular reversibility rather than a permanent loss of the kisspeptin system.

slides.title: Kiss2 administration changes pituitary gene expression
body: Zhang and colleagues administered **Kiss2-10**, the mature ten-amino-acid peptide, to sexually mature male lined seahorses. They then measured brain and pituitary transcripts at 3 and 6 hours, comparing peptide-treated animals with saline-treated controls. This intervention tested physiological responsiveness to the identified signal.

Pituitary FSHβ transcripts increased at 3 hours, and both FSHβ and LHβ increased at 6 hours. **Gonadotropins** are pituitary hormones regulating the gonads; FSH and LH are follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormone. Their beta-subunit transcripts identify components of those hormones.

The measured salmon-type gonadotropin-releasing hormone, sGnRH, and GPR54-2 transcripts did not increase. Pituitary gene responses can therefore occur without a parallel increase in these particular upstream transcripts over the sampled interval.

slides.title: Kiss2 administration raises circulating testosterone
body: **Testosterone** is a steroid hormone associated with reproductive physiology. Following Kiss2-10 administration, Zhang and colleagues collected blood from male lined seahorses at 3 and 6 hours and measured serum testosterone with an immunoassay. The saline-treated group provided the injection comparison.

Testosterone was elevated at 6 hours after peptide treatment. The same experimental series found increased pituitary gonadotropin transcripts, connecting the administered peptide to changes at more than one level of reproductive physiology.

The observations support endocrine responsiveness of mature males to Kiss2-10. A circulating hormone response and a tissue transcript response are different measurements, and their coordinated changes connect the identified peptide system to the reproductive axis.

slides.title: Vasotocin and isotocin occupy preoptic tissue
body: **Vasotocin** and **isotocin** are nine-amino-acid peptide hormones related to mammalian vasopressin and oxytocin. Zhang and colleagues cloned their precursors in lined seahorses and used in situ hybridization, a method detecting selected RNA sequences within tissue, to locate cells expressing the genes.

Both transcript signals occurred in the **preoptic area**, hypothalamic tissue associated with reproductive regulation. Vasotocin labeling was concentrated centrally, whereas isotocin labeling was more peripheral within the examined area. The preparations localized signaling-molecule transcripts to identifiable neural tissue.

The study also used a sense-probe control to assess nonspecific labeling. Transcript localization and the later vasotocin intervention supply complementary anatomical and physiological evidence for a seahorse neuroendocrine system.

slides.title: Vasotocin triggers premature release of young
body: **Parturition** is the release of offspring at the end of pregnancy. Zhang and colleagues injected pregnant lined seahorse males with vasotocin at 50 or 500 ng/g body mass and compared them with saline-injected controls. Treated males performed repeated body-swinging movements associated with birth.

The released young were premature: they were shorter and retained larger yolk sacs than normally released animals. **Yolk** is stored embryonic nutrition, and persistence of a large yolk sac identifies incomplete development at the time of release.

The peptide intervention therefore affected the timing of a reproductive behavior, not simply a molecular marker. Male seahorse birth combines bodily movement with an endocrine state that can be experimentally shifted by vasotocin administration.

slides.title: Pregnancy and birth involve distinct peptide responses
body: Male seahorse reproduction includes transitions into pregnancy and into birth, with different peptide-associated responses. Zhang and colleagues found reduced Kiss2 and receptor transcripts during pregnancy, followed by recovery after parturition. A separate vasotocin experiment shifted pregnant males toward premature release.

**Reproductive state** therefore changes both the molecular background and the response to a supplied signal. Kiss2 measurements describe stage-associated regulation, whereas vasotocin administration directly changes the timing of bodily birth behavior. The experimental designs address different parts of the cycle.

The released offspring begin visually guided feeding while their own sensory, neural, and skeletal systems continue developing. Parental endocrine timing and offspring developmental readiness meet at birth, linking adult reproductive control to juvenile behavioral independence.

items.text: Newborn lined seahorses capture live prey while retinal organization is already recognizable and snout ossification continues.
The prominent optic tectum and three-layered cerebellum differentiate during postnatal development.
A slow approach and quiet water region limit prey warning; a close-range pivot strike can reach prey in less than 1 ms.
Lined seahorses change abdominal luminance more strongly during familiar partner interactions, with most display events performed by males.
Kiss2-10 administration increases pituitary gonadotropin transcripts and later circulating testosterone in mature males.
Vasotocin administration induces premature offspring release and changes estrogen and pituitary transcript responses in pregnant males.
